seasons.review_body: Adapted from Jornn Lier Horst's novels The Caveman and The Hunting Dogs, the debut season of Wisting arrived on Viaplay and TV3 in April 2019 with Sven Nordin anchoring the series as William Wisting - a detective whose quiet authority never tips into cliche. The season pulls off a structural gambit most Nordic noirs avoid: it runs a Norwegian cold case investigation alongside a live FBI hunt, with Carrie-Anne Moss as Special Agent Maggie Griffin providing genuine transatlantic tension rather than an obvious American hook. Critics at Rotten Tomatoes gave the season 81 percent from 4 reviews. Dorothy Rabinowitz in the Wall Street Journal called every episode alive. Euan Ferguson in the Observer went further, calling it the best Nordic noir ever made. Premiere viewership broke Viaplay streaming records with over 250,000 viewers per episode across platforms.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Wisting S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The television is still on. That is the first ugly fact that matters. The show lets the set keep glowing inside a life that ended months earlier, then lets **Hammer** put the horror into one plain detail: three months of TV while a man mummified in place. Wisting begins as a death investigation, but the episode's colder idea cuts deeper. Information keeps arriving, and each new answer makes the case less stable.

## A Dead Man, a Running Television

The opening minutes place a self-help phrase on screen: “LOOK AFTER YOURSELF,” followed by “A COURSE ON SELF-REALIZATION.” It is a neat cruelty, because the hour that follows is about a person nobody looked after in time. BollyAI's read: the premiere understands that a procedural does not need to shout when the image is already doing the work.

The television detail is the first major piece of craft. Hammer's line about the TV being on for three months gives the case a clock without turning it into a lecture. It also gives the detectives something better than atmosphere: an investigative lead. “What channel? What was he watching?” turns a macabre image into police work. That is where the premiere is at its best. It takes a bleak discovery and asks how the physical world around it can talk.

The tone is patient to the point of severity. The dossier notes long quiet gaps near the beginning and again around the early-middle stretch, and the episode uses those spaces to make later bursts of information feel procedural rather than melodramatic. The risk is clear: this is a dry way to open a crime series. The benefit is stronger. By refusing to overplay the corpse, the hour makes the room feel examined instead of exploited.

## Secrecy Becomes the First Suspect

The first institutional instinct is containment. Until the identity is known, the line is simple: “Nothing until we know the identity.” That choice gives the episode its early moral pressure. The police are not hiding the case for cheap suspense. They are trying to keep facts clean before names harden into public truth.

That matters because Wisting S1E1 is built around unstable identification. The body, the fingerprints, the plastic bag, the missing elderly North American, the biblical ship, the wanted US man: each clue seems to clarify the story, then pushes it sideways. The episode's thesis sits there. This is a case about evidence that points with confidence before the full picture is ready to obey.

**Alfheim** becomes the clearest example of that tension. fingerprints on a plastic bag identify a wanted man in the US as **Robert Godwin**. The episode gives the moment a jolt because physical evidence feels clean. Fingerprints sound like finality. Yet the central contradiction in the dossier is that the investigation cannot be 100 percent sure it is Godwin, even as the evidence seems to name him.

That tension is good procedural writing. The premiere does not treat forensic detail as magic. It treats it as leverage, and leverage can bend the wrong way if applied too early.

## Robert Godwin Is an Answer That Makes Things Worse

The Godwin thread gives the hour its international charge. A wanted US man may have been hiding in Norway under another identity, and the thought changes the scale of the case without changing the show's temperature. The episode does not suddenly become a chase. It stays in rooms, conversations, reports, and controlled exchanges of information.

That restraint mostly works. Once Godwin is named, the show could have inflated the episode into a louder hunt. Instead, it lets the investigation assemble around absence. A North American elderly man rented a house and disappeared. A biblical ship becomes part of the connection. The plastic bag holds fingerprints. Then the DNA report arrives and knocks the case into a new shape: the body is **Peter Crabb**.

That beat works because it is not played as a twist for its own sake. It is a reframe. The body in the chair becomes a doorway into Godwin's possible victims, aliases, movements, and methods. The episode earns that turn by making every earlier detail provisional.

The weakness is that the middle section can feel more functional than gripping. The FBI logistics and evidence updates generate urgency, but the dialogue-heavy construction sometimes leaves the drama trapped inside case status. BollyAI's read: the hour has a firm spine, though some of its connective tissue is all briefing and no bite.

## Line Pulls the Case Toward the Press

**Line Wisting** gives the premiere a second pressure point. Her contradiction is clean: she wants reporting access while remaining entangled with the investigation. The dossier notes that she gets keys and later appears in connection with missing-woman leads. That is enough to make her more than a side character orbiting the police plot.

Her presence matters because the episode is obsessed with information control. The authorities want operational boundaries. They are told the case is not for town, not for home, and not for the press. Line's role presses directly against that rule. The show plants a family and professional conflict without needing to spell out every consequence yet.

This is where the premiere widens its map. The question expands beyond the dead man's identity into access: who gets to know, who gets to ask, and who might damage the case by being right too early. The procedural mood benefits from that complication, because secrecy without an opposing force can go inert. Line supplies the friction.

The hour does not fully cash that thread yet. It plants it. That is acceptable for a premiere, but it also means Line's material reads more like a fuse than an explosion. The interesting part is the placement. She is close enough to touch the case, and that closeness already looks dangerous.

## The Wells Turn the Premiere Darker

The final major movement pushes the investigation backward across decades. The instruction to check open cases of missing young women dating back 20 years changes the shape of the episode. Godwin becomes more than a hidden man. He becomes a possible method, a pattern, a history.

The wells are the bleakest image in the dossier. They turn concealment into geography. If victims may have been hidden in old wells, then the landscape itself becomes evidence. That is a strong late-premiere move because it makes the case feel larger without relying on spectacle. The show has spent the hour on bodies, bags, fingerprints, DNA, and withheld names. Now it gives those details a burial system.

**Ellen Robekk**, mentioned as the missing colleague's niece, becomes the emotional question inside that system. Will she be found alive, or does the well lead point somewhere worse? The episode does not answer, and that is the right kind of open loop for a first chapter. It is specific, grounded, and grim enough to justify the next hour.

The title may simply be “Episode 1,” but the design is more precise than that. It starts with a corpse nobody noticed for months and ends with the possibility that many others have been hidden for years. The premiere's best move is that expansion. One dead man in a chair becomes a map of absence.

## The Verdict

Wisting S1E1 is a controlled procedural opener with a strong central engine: every new fact narrows the case and destabilizes it at the same time. The television, the fingerprints, the DNA report, the Godwin connection, and the wells each move the investigation forward while proving that certainty is the most dangerous mood in the room. The episode's restraint is its identity, though that same restraint leaves parts of the middle feeling dutiful rather than charged. BollyAI's read: this is a 7.4 hour. It lacks dazzle, but it is clean enough to trust. As a season starter, it plants the right machinery: a hidden fugitive, a dead man with the wrong first answer, a reporter too close to the case, and a landscape that may be carrying bodies.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

bollymeter.basis: Condensed to 4 episodes, Season 2 maintains the procedural quality but loses the sprawl that made Season 1 exceptional. Based on The Inner Darkness.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 (adapting Horst's The Inner Darkness) aired as a 4-episode run on Viaplay from late December 2021. The compressed format - half the episode count of Season 1 - means the investigation moves faster but breathes less. Sven Nordin remains the moral gravity of the series, and the Larvik winter landscape continues to do atmospheric work that most crime dramas spend a budget trying to manufacture. Carrie-Anne Moss returns, keeping the FBI thread alive. The season functions as a satisfying case-closed chapter rather than an expansion of the first season's ambitions.
seasons.season_over_season: Shorter and tighter than Season 1, Season 2 trades the first season's slow-burn sprawl for a focused 4-episode case - effective but narrower in scope.

seasons.review_body: Season 3, based on Horst's The Hunting Dogs novel, continued the 4-episode format that the series adopted after its debut season. The story focuses on a cold case that implicates figures inside the police force - a structural choice that raises the stakes for Wisting personally. The compact runtime serves this more introspective arc well, keeping the investigation taut without overstaying its welcome.
seasons.season_over_season: Turns the procedural lens inward as Season 3 implicates law enforcement itself, adding personal cost to what had been Wisting's professional mission.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 arrived in March 2024 adapting Horst's A Question of Guilt, continuing the compressed 4-episode structure that became the series' post-debut format. BBC iPlayer coverage described the writing as having genius-level craft, and the season drew strong online attention as the final arc of the series began to take shape. The Larvik setting and Nordin's performance remain the anchors.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 deepens the personal dimension of Wisting's cases as the series builds toward its conclusion.

seasons.review_body: The fifth and final season aired in September 2024 on Viaplay, with Sven Nordin confirming it as his farewell to the Wisting role. Shelley Conn of Bridgerton guest-starred, broadening the series' international dimension for the final run. The season closes out the five-year arc that began with the FBI crossover in 2019 - a proper send-off for a procedural that, at its peak, held the Nordic noir crown.
seasons.season_over_season: The series finale season delivers a proper send-off for Nordin's Wisting, trading procedural tension for character resolution after five seasons.
